title: Captive Primordial Black Holes Could Trigger Detectable Stellar Explosions
excerpt: Simulations reveal that an asteroid-mass primordial black hole captured by a sun-like star could consume its host and produce detectable multiwavelength emissions.
content:
Theoretical physicists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and collaborating institutions have modeled a novel mechanism through which astronomers could detect primordial black holes by observing the destruction of stars that capture them. Primordial black holes are minute, hypothetical entities proposed to have formed during the fraction of a second following the Big Bang, when tiny, high-density pockets collapsed under their own intense gravitational pull. If these microscopic relics exist, researchers suspect they could represent a substantial component of dark matter, the invisible substance accounting for the vast majority of matter in the universe.

According to research published in The Astrophysical Journal, the investigative team performed analytic calculations alongside three-dimensional numerical simulations based on equations governing general relativity, hydrodynamics, stellar evolution, and particle physics. Their models evaluated how an asteroid-mass primordial black hole would interact dynamically with a modern, sun-like star. The simulations demonstrated that while the smallest primordial black holes would have evaporated over cosmic time via Hawking radiation, heavier specimens roughly the mass of an asteroid—approximately one millionth of the mass of Earth—and the physical size of an atom would survive into the modern epoch.

The study determined that the gravitational field of an isolated star is insufficient to capture a passing primordial black hole on its own. However, the researchers discovered that a three-body configuration involving a companion, such as a second star or a planet, can efficiently trap the passing object. In such configurations, the black hole experiences dynamic friction as it passes repeatedly through the outer stellar envelope. Over a span of thousands to millions of years, these recurrent passages gradually diminish the orbital radius, ultimately causing the black hole to settle directly into the center of the host star.

Once situated within the stellar core, the black hole begins an internal accretion phase. The growth rate of the black hole is governed by the quantity of energy released back into the surrounding stellar gas, which heats the medium and counteracts subsequent infall. The simulations revealed that the majority of this energy is transported directly into the black hole rather than remaining in the ambient medium. Consequently, the core object grows considerably faster than earlier calculations had estimated, consuming approximately one percent of the host star’s total mass over several million years.

As the black hole expands to several meters in diameter, stellar rotation begins to dictate the geometry of the infall. If the host star possesses sufficient angular velocity, the surrounding gas can no longer fall directly past the event horizon. Instead, the material accumulates into a rapidly rotating accretion disk centered on the spinning black hole at the heart of the star. As lead author Ore Gottlieb noted, the formation of this rotating disk establishes an irreversible sequence that seals the physical fate of the host star.

The interactions within this interior system proceed rapidly once the disk becomes established. As the spinning black hole consumes material spiraling inward from the disk, it twists the local spacetime metric and alters the configuration of the disk’s internal magnetic fields. These twisted magnetic fields subsequently channel plasma and power collimated, highly energetic electromagnetic jets emanating from the rotational poles of the black hole. Within a few dozen seconds, these jets accelerate outward and completely rupture the host star, culminating in a catastrophic stellar explosion.

The research team calculated the resulting multiwavelength signature, determining that the explosion generates an initial flash of blue and ultraviolet light alongside high-energy X-rays and gamma rays. Over subsequent temporal intervals, the expanding outflow transitions to emit optical and infrared radiation, eventually producing lingering radio emissions. According to the team’s theoretical calculations, this energetic multiwavelength transient would attain sufficient luminosity to be registered by contemporary astronomical observatories across cosmological distances, even if originating in distant external galaxies.

The authors emphasize that identifying such an event requires distinguishing it from other energetic astrophysical transients that could produce comparable flashes of light. Astronomers encountering such a transient would need to analyze contextual markers, such as determining that the progenitor star possessed a mass and evolutionary state that should not naturally undergo a core-collapse explosion. Validating the occurrence of an internally consumed star would offer observational constraints on the spatial abundance of asteroid-mass primordial black holes and clarify their viability as candidates for dark matter.

The research was conducted by lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, alongside theoretical physicists from several partner institutions. Co-authors include Matteo Cantiello of the Flatiron Institute, Cameron Norton and Matthew Kleban of New York University, and Ken Van Tilburg of Stanford University. Appearing in The Astrophysical Journal under the title “The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes,” the study received support from the National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science Advanced Scientific Computing Research Program. Together, the collaborating researchers analyzed whether the interactions between ancient compact objects and modern stars could produce observable signatures capable of being detected by astronomers.

Scientists have hypothesized that primordial black holes formed during the fraction of a second following the Big Bang, when minute pockets of dense matter collapsed under their own gravity. If these relics exist today, they could account for a significant component of dark matter, the invisible substance making up most of the universe’s matter. However, the lightest primordial black holes would have disappeared over cosmic epochs due to Hawking radiation, a quantum mechanism proposed by physicist Stephen Hawking whereby black holes slowly emit energy and shrink. In contrast, heavier primordial black holes would not have had sufficient time to disappear. These persisting relics are predicted to possess masses comparable to an asteroid, roughly one millionth the mass of Earth, while remaining compressed to the physical size of an atom.

To investigate how these lingering asteroid-mass relics might interact with stars in the modern universe, the team formulated detailed theoretical calculations and three-dimensional simulations. Their modeling framework combined fundamental equations from general relativity, hydrodynamics, stellar evolution, and particle physics. Gottlieb and his colleagues evaluated what would occur if an atom-sized primordial black hole encountered a modern, sun-like star, examining the physical conditions required for capture and subsequent evolution. The researchers sought to determine whether this dynamic process could generate distinct signals bright enough for astronomers to detect using existing telescopic instruments, thereby providing an empirical pathway to confirm the physical existence of primordial black holes.

The calculations revealed that the gravitational pull from an isolated star is not enough to trap a passing primordial black hole. Instead, the researchers discovered that capture requires a three-body configuration involving a companion, such as a second star or planet. Within this arrangement, gravitational interaction efficiently traps the passing black hole. As the black hole repeatedly traverses stellar material, it experiences friction that steadily saps its motion. Over a span of thousands to millions of years, these recurrent passages gradually shrink its orbit. Although extensive in human terms, this timespan is nearly instantaneous on cosmic timescales, culminating when the black hole falls directly into the center of the star.

Once settled into the stellar core, the black hole begins devouring the star from the inside. The team modeled how rapidly the object grows, noting that accretion speed depends on how much energy is released back into the surrounding star as it heats the gas and slows further infall. The simulations demonstrated that most of this energy is carried directly into the black hole, allowing it to grow faster than previously thought. Over several million years, the black hole consumes roughly one percent of the star’s mass, expanding to a size of a few meters. If the star spins fast enough, stellar gas cannot fall directly into the black hole. Instead, the gas piles up into a rotating disk around the few-meter-sized black hole, a state that Gottlieb described as essentially a death sentence for the star.

With the accretion disk established, the final stage unfolds with extreme speed. The central black hole is also spinning, twisting surrounding space and time as it consumes the disk’s spiraling matter. This continuous infall twists and pulls on the disk’s magnetic field lines, powering exceptionally strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole. Within a few dozen seconds, these powerful jets pierce completely through the star, causing it to explode. The team’s theoretical models showed that this catastrophic event releases enormous energy across space, transitioning from internal accretion into an explosive outburst within a matter of moments.

The researchers calculated the complete electromagnetic signature generated by this explosion, evaluating the color and intensity of light produced across the spectrum. The blast initially emits X-rays and gamma rays alongside a luminous flash of blue and ultraviolet light bright enough to be detected by current telescopes. As the outflow evolves, emissions transition into optical and infrared light, followed later by radio emissions. Gottlieb pointed out that because other astrophysical phenomena can generate a similar flash, astronomers must look for specific corroborating clues, such as an explosion occurring in a star of a mass that is not supposed to explode. Identifying such an internal parasite provides an observational method to place constraints on primordial black holes and evaluate their contribution to dark matter.
